problem: General-purpose robots that combine LLM reasoning with navigation and grasping lack open-source, modular frameworks with robust failure handling; plans fail without recovery, especially in sequential multi-step tasks.
motivation: Embodied AI is moving robots from specialized systems to general agents adapting to dynamic environments. LLM-based planners are brittle when execution fails, and rigid pipelines are hard to extend or port to other platforms. Only the abstract is available, so details are limited.
key_idea: An open-source modular embodied framework that couples an LLM planner with semantic perception, navigation and grasping modules, and uses LLM feedback for re-planning (re-execution, refinement, exploration) when failures occur.
insight: Per the abstract, LLM-feedback re-planning raises success from 50% to 90% on single-directive tasks and from 6% to 70% on sequential tasks, so error recovery matters most for long-horizon tasks where failures compound. The modular design lets components be swapped for other platforms. No ablation details are available.
method: LLM high-level reasoning: an LLM decomposes instructions into tasks for the robot modules (details not available from the abstract)
Re-planning mechanism: LLM feedback handles failures via re-execution, refinement and exploration strategies
Semantic perception module: supplies scene semantics that interact dynamically with the re-planner
Navigation module: low-level navigation control executing planned subgoals
Grasping module: low-level manipulation control for object grasping
Modular open-source architecture: components can be replaced or extended, enabling adaptation to other platforms

setting.backbone: LLM (unspecified in abstract) with modular perception, navigation and grasping components

numbers_note: abstract only; the abstract reports success-rate gains (50%->90% single-directive, 6%->70% sequential) but on no named benchmark, so no entries were recorded
results: Re-planning improves success from 50% to 90% on single-directive tasks and from 6% to 70% on sequential tasks, according to the abstract. Baselines and the benchmark are not named.
limitations: Evaluation appears limited to custom navigation and grasping tasks with no standard benchmark, per the abstract
Robustness, flexibility and cross-task generalization are left to a roadmap of future work
